owner.occupation: Coordinator at a neighbourhood house small-business program

world.bio: I'm the coordinator of the Women's Enterprise Program at Box Hill Neighbourhood House, in Melbourne's east. The program supports migrant women starting or running small businesses: catering, tailoring, hair, grocery. We run workshops, one-on-one mentoring and have a small pool of volunteers who help with admin and English. I've been in the role for three years.
skills_assets: Program budget for workshops and a part-time assistant (0.4 FTE)
A room for 20 people with projector, a small kitchen, a children's corner
Relationships with the City of Whitehorse council, Moneycorp, and a free legal advice service
A volunteer pool of about 30, most are retirees or university students
Free places in the neighbourhood house's conversational English class for all volunteers
Fluent English, Tamil and Hindi, conversational Mandarin (poor)

projects.name: English Bookkeeping Workshop (Term 4)
projects.text: Eight-week workshop for women running small shops, covering invoices, GST, BAS and basic bookkeeping in Xero. Currently 12 enrolled but attendance has dropped. Three owners of Chinese grocery shops have dropped out; they say the English terms are too much.

projects.name: Volunteer retention
projects.text: We keep losing volunteers to paid jobs, especially the uni students and the early retirees. Trying to create a pathway: volunteers get free English classes and a reference letter after 40 hours.

notes.text: Term 4 planning. We have 12 women enrolled in the bookkeeping workshop, but three of the Chinese grocery owners (Mrs. Wu, Mrs. Zhang, Ms. Huang) dropped after week 2. They said it's too hard to follow the English terms. I called Mrs. Wu. She said 'Priya, I understand numbers, I just don't understand your words'. That sentence has been stuck in my head.

Volunteer meeting. Five of thirty turned up. One said she got a job at Woolworths and will leave in October. Another said her uni exams are coming. Another just stopped replying. We lose them at the point they become useful. Not their fault.

Planning my wedding. Budget $18,000, which is both generous and nothing. My fiancé Leo wants a backyard wedding, I want a hall. We settled on a hall with a backyard. His mother wants 120 guests; we want 60. We're still negotiating the guest list, which is basically diplomacy.

Wrote in our internal notes: what we need is a Mandarin-speaking volunteer who actually understands accounts. Not a bilingual volunteer who can read a menu, someone who can sit with Mrs. Wu and translate BAS into her own language, line by line. I've tried the council's interpreter service, it's a stranger for one hour. It has to be a recurring person.

Surf lesson at Torquay. Fell off the board nine times, stood up once. The instructor said 'that's a good ratio for a beginner'. I laughed so hard I swallowed half the ocean. It's the only time I'm not thinking about the program.

Fostering two kittens from the RSPCA: Chai and Biscuit. They knocked over the plant, ate part of my notes, slept on the laptop. Leo says no more kittens. I said it's temporary. He said you said that about the last ones.

Updated the volunteer brochure. Added: 'Volunteers receive a free place in the neighbourhood house's Conversational English class, a reference letter after 40 hours, and morning tea.' I'm particularly proud of the last one. Nothing keeps people better than good biscuits.

Mrs. Wu's daughter called, saying her mother wants to try again if the workshop is in Mandarin. We can't afford to run a separate class. But maybe one person, sitting next to her, would be enough. Need to find them.

messages.text: Mrs. Wu: Priya, I will not come to the class again. Me: Mrs. Wu, I understand. Mrs. Wu: It is not you. It is the words. Me: Would you come if someone could explain in Mandarin? Mrs. Wu: Maybe. Me: I'll try to find someone.
Leo: Mum wants to invite her entire choir. Me: How many? Leo: Thirty. Me: No. Leo: I told her. She said 'I'll bring the choir anyway'. Me: Of course she did.
Jenny: Priya, I got the job at the library. Me: Congratulations! Jenny: I'm sorry to leave. Me: Don't be sorry. You've done great. Jenny: Do you have someone to replace me? Me: Working on it.
Rob: Next year's funding review is in March. Me: What do you need from me? Rob: Numbers. Participants, completion rates, outcomes. Me: Completion rates are not great this term. Rob: Then explain why.

relations.about: Runs a Chinese grocery in Box Hill; 62; understands accounts but not English terms
City of Whitehorse council officer, supportive but needs numbers

constraints: Program budget is fixed until June, cannot pay volunteers
Can only offer non-monetary benefits (English class, references)
Mandarin-speaking support must be recurring, not one-off interpreter
Limited staff time, 0.4 FTE assistant only
sensitive: Anxious about funding review in March
